concepts.one_line: A score from $-1$ to $+1$ that asks whether predictions land on the line $y = x$, not merely whether they rise and fall together.
concepts.explain:
An ordinary correlation only asks whether two series move together. A prediction that is always exactly half the true value correlates perfectly, because whenever the truth goes up the prediction goes up. That is not what a rating prediction needs to be right.

The concordance correlation coefficient measures agreement instead of association. It is the correlation multiplied by a penalty, and the penalty grows whenever the two series differ in their mean or in their spread. A model that tracks the shape of a visitor's ratings but sits systematically too high, or swings too narrowly, is marked down for it.

Zero is the value a model scores when it carries no information about the held-out person. Negative values are possible and mean the predictions disagree with the ratings more than a flat line would.
concepts.here: Every prediction in this thesis is scored by $\mathrm{CCC}$, computed per held-out visitor and then averaged. Experiment 1's twenty cells fall between $-0.072$ and $+0.084$. Experiment 2's four alignment arms average between $+0.018$ and $+0.024$.
concepts.example: Take a visitor whose arousal ratings and predictions correlate at $\rho = 0.5$, which sounds usable. If the predictions have half the spread of the ratings, the penalty term drags the concordance down to roughly $0.4$, and if they also sit one scale point too high it falls further. This is why a correlation reported alone overstates how well a model predicts a rating.
pitfalls: A high correlation does not imply a high CCC. Check the means and the spreads before believing one.
CCC is computed within each visitor here, then averaged. Pooling every visitor's rows first would let between-person differences inflate it.

concepts.one_line: Train on everyone except one person, predict that person, repeat until every person has had a turn.
concepts.explain:
The question this thesis asks is whether a model can predict the affect of a visitor it has never seen. An evaluation must therefore never let a visitor's own data reach the model that scores them.

Ordinary cross-validation shuffles rows, so seconds from the same visitor land in both the training and the test half. A model can then recognise the person rather than the state, and the score looks far better than the model deserves. Leave-one-subject-out removes that possibility by splitting on the person instead of on the row.

The cost is that each fold trains on a small cohort and is scored on one person, so the fold-to-fold spread is wide. That spread is a real property of the problem, not noise to be smoothed away.
concepts.here: Every score in this thesis uses it, with 22 visitors in the rcea stream and 16 in retro. The spread across visitors within one cell runs from $0.045$ to $0.110$, which is ten to twenty times the difference between the methods being compared.

concepts.one_line: The average, across the ordered levels, of how often each level is correctly recovered, so a model cannot look good just by guessing the biggest level every time.
concepts.explain:
Plain accuracy counts what fraction of predictions were right. On a lopsided target, where one level holds most of the rows, a model that always predicts that level scores high on plain accuracy while never actually distinguishing anything.

Balanced accuracy fixes this by scoring each level's own recall separately, the fraction of that level's true rows the model actually recovered, and then averaging those recalls across levels rather than across rows. A level with ten rows counts exactly as much as a level with a thousand.

Its floor is not zero. It is $1/B$ for $B$ levels, because a model guessing uniformly at random gets any one level right about a $1/B$ share of the time. Comparing a score against $1/B$ rather than against zero is what lets a change in the level count be read fairly: a finer scale scores lower for a purely arithmetic reason even from a model that has not gotten any worse.
concepts.here: This thesis reports balanced accuracy as the cross-check on the headline \ac{QWK} figure for every binned target from Experiment 3 onward, always read against its own chance value of $1/B$ rather than a fixed threshold, since $B$ itself changes across the level-count sweep of 3, 4, 5, 10, 12, 15, 18 and 20. It is also the figure the dataset's origin, van der Kaaden, scored his own four classifiers on: about $0.84$ trained and tested on the same person, collapsing to $0.20$ to $0.24$ for the tree models he emphasised under leave-one-subject-out, and as low as $0.10$ for the simplest of the four.
concepts.example: With five levels, chance is $1/5 = 0.20$. A model that recovers level 1 perfectly but never predicts levels 2 through 5 correctly scores a recall of $1.0$ on level 1 and $0.0$ on the rest, for a balanced accuracy of $0.20$: exactly chance, even though its plain accuracy could look inflated by however many rows happen to sit in level 1.
pitfalls: A balanced accuracy above zero is not the same as above chance; the reference is $1/B$, and $1/B$ shrinks every time the sweep moves to a finer level count.
Comparing balanced accuracy at two different level counts directly compares two different chance floors; read each count against its own $1/B$ instead.

concepts.one_line: An agreement score for ordered levels that punishes being three levels off nine times harder than being one level off, because the distance between prediction and truth is squared.
concepts.explain:
Plain accuracy on ordered levels treats every wrong answer the same: predicting one level too high counts exactly as bad as predicting four levels too high. For a rating that runs from calm to excited, those two mistakes are not equally bad, and a score built for unordered categories cannot tell them apart.

Quadratic weighted kappa starts from ordinary kappa, an agreement score already corrected for the agreement two raters would reach by chance, and adds a weight to every possible disagreement equal to the squared distance between the two levels involved, divided by the largest possible squared distance. A miss of one level barely counts against the score; a miss of half the scale counts heavily.

Because the weighting and the chance correction are both baked in, a model that just repeats the most common level, or that reproduces the level distribution without tracking any individual row, scores close to zero rather than looking falsely good. The measure is nonetheless sensitive to the range of levels used and to how unevenly they are filled, which is why this thesis never relies on it alone.
concepts.here: \ac{QWK} is the headline figure for every ordinal result in this thesis from Experiment 3 onward, computed once, pooled over all held-out visitors' predictions for a slice, rather than averaged fold by fold. The discussion chapter reports that fitting a classifier directly on the binned levels costs between $0.0587$ and $0.1046$ \ac{QWK} against reading a continuous prediction into levels after the fact, on every slice, which is part of why the post-hoc arm was the one carried forward rather than the classifier trained on levels.
concepts.example: On a 5-level scale ($B=5$), predicting level 3 when the truth is level 4 costs a weight of $(3-4)^2/4^2 = 0.0625$. Predicting level 1 when the truth is level 4 costs $(1-4)^2/4^2 = 0.5625$: nine times as much, for being three levels off instead of one.
pitfalls: A QWK computed pooled across every held-out visitor is not the same number as the average of each visitor's own QWK; state which one is being reported.

QWK moves whenever the level marginals move, so restricting to attended-painting rows or recentring a visitor's own scale can shift it for reasons that have nothing to do with any second being predicted better. This thesis reports the continuous CCC alongside it for exactly that reason.

concepts.one_line: The score a model would get by carrying no real information about the person being predicted, which every result in this thesis is measured against instead of against a fixed pass mark.
concepts.explain:
A positive-looking score is tempting to read as evidence a model works. But "positive" only means something once it is clear what a model with nothing to say would score, and that reference point differs from metric to metric.

For \ac{CCC} and \ac{QWK}, that reference is exactly zero: both are constructed so that a prediction carrying no real relationship to the truth lands around zero, and both can fall below it when a prediction actively disagrees with the truth. For balanced accuracy the reference is $1/B$, since guessing uniformly among $B$ levels gets one right about a $1/B$ share of the time by luck alone.

This thesis leans on the idea harder than most projects do, because its central finding is that scores sit at this floor rather than above it. Experiment 1's twenty sensor-by-slice cells run from $-0.072$ to $+0.084$ \ac{CCC}, straddling zero rather than clearing it, and that pattern is read as "none of the five sensors recovers a usable amount" rather than as a small positive effect.

A chance-corrected floor is a different idea from the selection resolution (its own entry). The floor says what "nothing" looks like; the resolution says how far above or below "nothing" a score has to sit before it stops being read as noise.
concepts.here: Every scoring decision in this thesis names its floor before comparing anything to it: zero for \ac{CCC} and \ac{QWK}, $1/B$ for balanced accuracy. The discussion chapter's phrase for it, "chance-corrected floor", is used throughout to describe where scores landed rather than whether they were merely positive or negative.
concepts.example: A model scoring $\mathrm{CCC}=+0.03$ sounds like it has found something. But the floor is $0$, and the measured run-to-run spread of this exact pipeline is $0.08$ in either direction (the selection resolution), so $+0.03$ sits well inside the band a model with no real signal would land in by chance alone.
pitfalls: A positive number is not evidence of a working model on its own; it has to clear both the chance-corrected floor and the selection resolution before it counts as a real effect.
Balanced accuracy's floor moves with the level count ($1/B$), so a raw number cannot be compared across a level-count sweep without first reading it against its own floor.

concepts.term: Root mean squared error, against CCC
concepts.one_line: The typical size of a prediction's miss, in the rating's own units, which says nothing on its own about whether that miss is a fixable bias or a real failure to track the person at all.
concepts.explain:
Root mean squared error answers a direct question: on average, how far off was the prediction? Every error is squared, the squares are averaged, and the square root brings the number back onto the rating's own scale, so an RMSE of $1.2$ means predictions typically miss by about $1.2$ points on a $0$ to $10$ scale.

That directness hides two problems for a task like this one. First, RMSE carries no built-in reference for "no information": a model can post a deceptively small RMSE just by predicting close to the rating's own mean every time, especially on an axis whose ratings barely move, without tracking the visitor's actual ups and downs at all. Second, RMSE is not comparable across two axes or two sensors whose ratings have different spread. An axis with low variance makes any model look better by RMSE, for reasons that have nothing to do with prediction skill.

\ac{CCC} folds both problems away at once, by comparing the prediction against the true rating's own mean and spread before scoring it, so it already contains what a bare RMSE would need a separate baseline model to establish.
concepts.here: This thesis does not report RMSE anywhere. \ac{CCC} is used in its place for exactly the reasons above, given ratings whose spread differs by axis, by annotation stream, and by visitor. Where RMSE-style reasoning would still apply, it is folded into the CCC formula's own penalty term instead (see the CCC entry).
concepts.example: Retrospective arousal sits close to a flat line for many visitors: the data-characterisation chapter calls it "near-degenerate, almost piecewise-constant". A model predicting the session mean every second could post a small RMSE there purely because the target barely moves, while its CCC would sit close to zero, because it carries no real correlation with the visitor's own ups and downs.
pitfalls: A small RMSE on a low-variance axis, like retrospective arousal, is not evidence of a working model; check the axis's own spread before trusting the number.
RMSE cannot be compared across sensors or axes with different rating variance without first controlling for that variance, which is exactly what CCC already does.

concepts.one_line: Picking a model's settings only on the training participants of a fold, never on the visitor that fold is about to score, so the number that judges the model is not the number that picked it.
concepts.explain:
Every model family here carries settings that have to be chosen: how deep a tree grows, how hard a ridge penalty shrinks, and so on. The obvious way to choose them is to try a few options and keep whichever scores best on the data at hand. Done carelessly, that is also the fastest way to an inflated score, because the same data that judged the option is the data that picked it.

Nested cross-validation keeps the two jobs apart. Inside each \ac{LOSO} fold's training participants, a further split, the inner loop, tries each candidate setting and picks a winner. That winner is then refit on the whole training fold and scored, for the first and only time, on the held-out visitor, the outer loop. The held-out visitor never appears in the inner loop, so nothing about the chosen settings can have adapted to that visitor's particular data.

Skipping the inner loop, tuning once on everyone and reusing the same setting in every fold, looks harmless from the outside and is one of the most common ways a LOSO pipeline that looks leakage-free still overstates itself: the chosen setting has quietly been fit to the very visitors it will later be scored on.
concepts.here: Every one of the eight model families in Experiment 1 carries a three-candidate hyperparameter grid, tuned by a nested search inside every training fold. Ridge, being cheap to fit, tunes on an inner leave-one-subject-out split of its own; the tree, boosting, and kernel families tune on a cheaper inner five-fold split grouped by participant. The winning setting is refit on the full training fold and scored only then, on the one visitor nothing in the inner loop has seen.
concepts.example: For the fold that holds out one rcea visitor, the inner loop for ridge regression runs its own miniature leave-one-out over the other 21 rcea visitors to pick the penalty strength. Only after that choice is fixed does the model see the held-out visitor's rows at all, and only to be scored, never to be trained or tuned.
pitfalls: Tuning once on the whole cohort and reusing that setting across every fold is a leak, even though it looks identical to nested tuning from the outside; the setting has still seen every visitor it will later be tested on.

An inner loop that is itself too small can pick unstable settings by chance; this is part of why the tree, boosting and kernel families use a cheaper five-fold inner split rather than a full inner LOSO.

concepts.one_line: The gap in score two candidates need before this thesis will call one of them better, measured from how much the pipeline's own repeats disagree with each other before any candidate is ever compared to another.
concepts.explain:
Any pipeline with randomness in it, a random forest's bootstrap sample, a fold's tie-breaking, gives a slightly different score every time it is rerun on identical data under identical settings. Comparing two real candidates without first knowing how much that pure noise moves the score risks reading noise as a discovery.

This thesis measures that noise directly instead of assuming it away. One fixed configuration, the random forest on cardiac features against rcea arousal, is passed through the entire leave-one-subject-out evaluation twenty times, changing nothing but the random seed and a resampling, with replacement, of each fold's training participants. The spread across those twenty repeat means is the pipeline's own run-to-run variability, and nothing else, since the data and the settings never change.

The gap between the fifth and ninety-fifth percentile of that spread, rounded up to two decimal places, becomes the resolution. Once fixed, that single number governs every later comparison in the thesis: two configurations, two model families, two alignment methods, two level counts. Anything closer together than the resolution is not read as a winner and a loser; it is read as a tie, and a tie is resolved toward the simpler or more conservative candidate rather than toward whichever happened to score marginally higher.
concepts.here: The resolution is measured once, in advance, on the random forest against rcea arousal with cardiac features, repeated twenty times: the twenty repeat means run from $-0.031$ to $+0.074$ \ac{CCC}, and their fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles differ by $0.078$, rounded up to $0.08$. Every later selection in the thesis, the fixation rule, the \ac{EDA} decomposition, the model family, the alignment method, the fusion mechanism, the level count, is read against that same $0.08$.
concepts.example: CatBoost's mean CCC across Experiment 1's twenty cells is $+0.0062$ and extremely randomised trees' is $+0.0055$, a gap of $0.0007$, about a hundredth of the $0.08$ resolution. The two are read as tied rather than as CatBoost winning, and the tie is resolved toward the family whose scores vary least across the twenty cells.
pitfalls: A candidate that scores numerically higher is not automatically "better"; check the gap against the resolution before calling it a win.

The resolution was measured on one fixed cell chosen in advance, before any real comparison was made, so it cannot be re-measured on whichever comparison one wants to win. Using a different cell to justify a different margin would defeat the point of measuring it at all.

concepts.one_line: Whether a model can predict someone it has already met is a different question from whether it can predict someone it has never met, and the same data can answer the two questions very differently.
concepts.explain:
A model trained and tested on rows from the same people, just different seconds of their visit, only ever has to solve a narrower problem: recognise this particular person's habits and settle into them. It can learn that this visitor's resting heart rate sits low, that this visitor's ratings rarely leave the top third of the scale, and lean on those personal habits without ever learning anything that would transfer to someone new.

Leave-one-subject-out removes that shortcut by construction, since the person being scored is never in the data the model trained on. If a within-participant split and a LOSO split give very different answers on the same features, the difference is telling you how much of the first score was really about recognising the person rather than about tracking the state.

The scale of that difference is the central fact this thesis works with. The dataset's origin scored his own four classifiers both ways: about $0.84$ balanced accuracy trained and tested on the same people, collapsing to $0.20$ to $0.24$ for the tree models he emphasised, and as low as $0.10$ for the simplest, once a person was genuinely held out. That is not a small effect of evaluation methodology; it is close to the entire signal a within-participant split reports.
concepts.here: Every research question in this thesis is deliberately posed under \ac{LOSO}, stated once and applied throughout: "each visitor is held out in turn, so no result rests on a person the model has already seen." This project's own from-scratch, leakage-free rebuild of the pipeline reproduced the same collapse three separate times as the raw-signal pipeline was rebuilt and recalibrated, landing at 0.139 to 0.226 balanced accuracy across models and conditions each time, inside the same near-chance band the dataset's origin reported.
concepts.example: A model given a visitor's resting heart rate could learn, purely from the training cohort, that a low resting rate tends to belong to one particular person who also happens to rate arousal high. That shortcut helps within-participant evaluation, where seconds from that same person sit in both halves of the split, but is worthless for a new visitor whose resting rate says nothing yet about how they rate anything.
pitfalls: A within-participant cross-validation split, rows shuffled at random, still leaks: seconds from the same visitor land in both train and test, so the model can learn the person rather than the state, and the score overstates what it can do for someone new.

The size of the within-person-to-LOSO gap matters less than which of the two a deployment actually needs; a guide meeting a visitor for the first time only ever needs the LOSO number, however good the within-person one looks.

concepts.one_line: A correlation that asks only whether two things rise and fall in the same order, not whether they rise and fall by the same amount, which matters when the numbers themselves are not on a shared scale.
concepts.explain:
An ordinary (Pearson) correlation compares the actual values of two series, and it works best when their relationship is close to a straight line. A single extreme reading can pull it around, and it has nothing sensible to say when the two series are related but bent rather than straight.

Spearman correlation sidesteps both problems by never looking at the raw values at all. Each series is first replaced by its own ranks, first smallest, second smallest, and so on, and the ordinary correlation is then computed on those ranks. What survives is only the order things came in; how far apart two readings were is thrown away entirely. That is exactly what a relationship needs to hold onto when a straight line is too strong an assumption, or when one visitor's rare high reading would otherwise dominate the whole coefficient.

It is also the natural choice for a person-relative rating. One visitor's "6" for arousal need not mean what another's "6" means, so comparing raw values across people is already shaky. But "this second was rated higher than that one" is a claim about order, and order is the one thing that survives the person-relative scale intact.
concepts.here: This thesis correlates every sensor feature against every rating axis by Spearman correlation, computed separately inside each visitor and only ever summarised afterward by its median and quartiles across visitors (see the within-participant-correlation entry). Across the 436 such tests, the median absolute coefficient runs from $0.02$ to $0.12$ depending on sensor and stream, and the single strongest, $-0.37$ for retrospective arousal, belongs to a confound in the recording apparatus rather than to a real relation with the rating.
concepts.example: For five paired readings, the two series are re-expressed as ranks 1 to 5 each, and the ordinary correlation formula is applied to the ranks instead of the raw numbers. A pair whose raw values sit at $(2, 9)$, $(3, 15)$, $(4, 15.5)$, $(4.2, 40)$, $(4.3, 41)$ correlates far less than perfectly under Pearson, because of the enormous jump at the end, but correlates at exactly $+1.0$ under Spearman, because every rank still rises together.
pitfalls: Spearman still assumes a monotonic relationship; a feature that rises then falls with the rating (a U shape) can score near zero despite carrying real information.

Tied values need a tie-aware version of the rank correlation, or the coefficient is subtly biased; rcea's step-like joystick trace, which can sit flat for long stretches, produces exactly this kind of tie.

concepts.one_line: Correlating a feature with a rating separately inside each visitor and then averaging those correlations is a different, safer question than throwing everyone's rows into one pile and correlating across all of them at once.
concepts.explain:
Pooling every visitor's rows together and computing one correlation treats every row as interchangeable, as though it made no difference which visitor a row came from. But two visitors can differ from each other, in resting physiology, in how they use the rating scale, more than either one varies across their own visit. If a feature's typical level differs between people who also happen to rate differently on average, that between-person difference alone can produce a pooled correlation that has nothing to do with how the feature moves within any one person's own experience.

Computing the correlation separately inside each visitor first, then summarising across the resulting per-visitor coefficients, removes that between-person difference from the picture entirely. Each visitor's own coefficient can only reflect what happened within that visitor's own session, since no other visitor's rows ever enter its computation.

This is precisely the mechanism Simpson's paradox names, and it matters here for more than technical hygiene: this thesis's own headline finding is that the between-person share of the affect ratings is large, $37\%$ to $65\%$ of the variance by the crossed mixed-effects decomposition, which is exactly the condition under which pooling would be most likely to manufacture a relationship that is not real.
concepts.here: Every feature-versus-rating correlation reported in Experiment 1 is computed within each visitor first: "these correlations are computed within each visitor rather than across the cohort, so that differences between people cannot appear as a relation." A feature only counts as related at all if its per-participant coefficients differ from zero under a paired test across participants, with the false-discovery rate controlled over every feature, axis and stream; none of the 436 such tests survives that correction.
concepts.example: Suppose calmer visitors also happen to keep a lower resting tonic \ac{EDA} level, and calmer visitors also happen to give lower arousal ratings on average, two plausible but unrelated facts about people rather than about moments. Pooling every row together could then produce a clear negative EDA-arousal correlation driven entirely by who is who, while the within-visitor correlations, computed one visitor at a time, could all sit near zero or even run positive.
pitfalls: Pooling all visitors' rows before correlating is one of the easiest ways to manufacture a relationship that really says "who is this person" rather than "what changed for them".

A within-participant coefficient still needs enough visitors contributing one before it means anything summarised; this thesis requires at least eight, and drops EDA on retro entirely for falling short of that.

concepts.one_line: A relationship can point one way inside every individual group and point the opposite way once the groups are pooled together, with nothing inside any single group having actually changed.
concepts.explain:
The textbook case is a university accused of favouring men in admissions: pooled across the whole university, men were admitted at a higher rate. Looked at department by department, women were admitted at an equal or higher rate in almost every one. What reversed the pooled figure was that women applied more often to the departments that admitted almost nobody, of either sex; the department someone applied to, not their sex, was driving the acceptance rate, and pooling hid that by mixing departments together.

The mechanism is always the same shape. Pooled data mixes two separate sources of variation: how two things move together inside a group, and how the groups themselves differ from each other on both things at once. When the second source is large and happens to run opposite to the first, the pooled number can flip sign entirely relative to what every single group shows on its own, without any group's own relationship having moved at all.

This is exactly the trap the within-participant-correlation entry is built to avoid, and it is why this thesis never pools visitors together before correlating anything. It is also why the variance decomposition of Experiment 4 explicitly separates a person share from a residual share rather than folding both into one pooled number: a model or a statistic that does not make that separation is implicitly betting that this reversal is not happening in its data, rather than checking.
concepts.here: This thesis structures its statistics around avoiding exactly this trap. Every feature-rating correlation is computed within participant and only ever summarised, never pooled, across the cohort (see within-participant-correlation). The crossed mixed-effects model of Experiment 4 applies the same logic to the ratings themselves, splitting variance into a person share, a painting share and a residual before any claim about a shared, cross-visitor signal is made.
concepts.example: If calmer visitors also happen to keep a lower resting skin-conductance level, and also happen to give lower arousal ratings on average, pooling every visitor's rows could show skin conductance falling as arousal falls, purely because of who those calm visitors are, even if not one of them shows any such relationship across their own seconds. The pooled line and every within-person line could point in opposite directions at once.
pitfalls: A strong pooled correlation is not evidence the effect exists for any one person; check whether it survives being computed one person at a time before trusting it.

The reversal can run either way: pooling can manufacture a relationship no individual shows, or hide a real one that every individual shows, depending on how the between-group differences happen to line up with the within-group ones.

concepts.one_line: A way of judging many simultaneous tests together that controls the share of the ones called significant which are actually false alarms, rather than trying to prevent any single false alarm from ever slipping through.
concepts.explain:
Run one test at the usual $p<0.05$ threshold and there is a $5\%$ chance of a false alarm if nothing real is there. Run four hundred such tests and, even if nothing real is there in any of them, about twenty are expected to look significant by chance alone, purely from running that many tests.

The traditional fix, Bonferroni correction, divides the threshold by the number of tests, which keeps the chance of even one false alarm across the whole batch low. That guarantee is bought at a steep price once the batch runs into the hundreds: real effects have to be very strong indeed to survive a threshold shrunk by a factor of four hundred.

The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure asks a different, more forgiving question. Instead of almost never allowing a single false alarm, it controls the expected proportion of false alarms among whichever tests end up called significant. The p-values are sorted from smallest to largest and compared against a threshold that rises with rank, so the harshest cutoff applies only to the single largest p-value that still gets to count, and every smaller one is judged more leniently. The result keeps a stated, tolerable share of the discoveries false, rather than making almost every individual test nearly impossible to pass.
concepts.here: Every sensor feature's correlation with a rating axis in Experiment 1 is one test among 436, and the false-discovery rate is controlled across all of them. None of the 436 survives correction, and the lowest adjusted $q$ value anywhere is $0.67$, even though fourteen individual tests would have passed the uncorrected $p<0.05$ threshold. Section~2 states the general rule this reflects throughout the thesis: "where many tests are run at once, the false-discovery rate is controlled."
concepts.formula: \text{for sorted } p_{(1)} \le \cdots \le p_{(m)}, \text{ find the largest } k \text{ with } p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{m}\alpha; \text{ reject } H_{(1)},\ldots,H_{(k)}
concepts.example: Among 400 tests at $\alpha=0.05$, the fifth-smallest p-value is compared not against $0.05$ but against $\frac{5}{400}\times 0.05 = 0.000625$. A p-value of $0.01$, comfortably significant on its own, fails that comparison and is not called a discovery, exactly the fate of most of this thesis's fourteen nominally significant tests once they were judged alongside the other 422.
pitfalls: A p-value that looks small in isolation, like $0.01$, can still fail after correction once it is judged against hundreds of other tests; check the corrected $q$ value, not the raw $p$, before calling anything a finding.

The correction is only as meaningful as the family of tests it is applied over; correcting fourteen promising-looking tests in isolation, after already discarding the rest, would understate how many chances those fourteen had to appear by luck.

concepts.one_line: A test for whether one thing tends to score higher than a paired other thing, built from the ranks of the differences rather than the raw differences themselves, so one extreme visitor cannot carry the result alone.
concepts.explain:
The paired t-test, the familiar way to compare two conditions measured on the same units, works by averaging the differences and asking whether that average sits far from zero. It assumes those differences are roughly bell-shaped, and a single visitor with an unusually large difference can pull the average, and the conclusion, around with it.

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test asks the same question a more robust way. For each paired unit, here each visitor, it takes the difference between the two scores being compared, ranks the absolute sizes of those differences from smallest to largest, and then compares the sum of ranks on the positive side against the sum on the negative side. If one condition genuinely tends to beat the other, the positive and negative differences will not split their rank-sum evenly; if the two conditions are really interchangeable, they will, regardless of how large or small any one visitor's difference happens to be.

Because the test works on ranks rather than raw sizes, a single visitor with a huge difference contributes only its rank, not its magnitude, to the result. That is exactly the property this thesis needs when comparing two settings across sixteen to twenty-two visitors whose scores can vary enormously in scale from one to the next.
concepts.here: Whether one setting beats another anywhere in this thesis is judged with a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over per-participant scores, each visitor contributing one paired difference. This is the test behind every headline comparison: alignment methods, fusion mechanisms, the localisation scoping comparison, and every personalisation lever against its own same-run reference, always with the false-discovery rate controlled across the family of tests run together.
concepts.example: Comparing two settings across six visitors' CCC scores, suppose five visitors show a small positive difference of about $0.01$ and one visitor shows a huge difference of $0.15$ in the same direction. A paired t-test's average would be dominated by that one visitor; the signed-rank test instead sees six positive differences out of six, a lopsided rank split regardless of how big the largest one was, and reaches the same conclusion either way.
pitfalls: The test needs enough paired visitors to have any power at all; per-participant \ac{QWK} in this thesis covers only 7 to 18 visitors per test, since a visitor whose ratings or predictions sit entirely in one level yields no kappa, which can leave a real effect unable to reach significance simply for lack of pairs.

A significant Wilcoxon result says the direction of the effect is unlikely to be chance; it says nothing about the size of the effect, which is why this thesis pairs it with a bootstrap confidence interval and the selection resolution before calling a difference real.

concepts.one_line: A single number for how much of the total spread in a measurement is a stable difference between the things being measured, people or paintings, rather than noise within any one of them.
concepts.explain:
An ordinary correlation compares exactly two paired columns, one rater's scores against another's. The intraclass correlation generalises that to any number of raters or repeats, and it is built directly out of a variance decomposition rather than out of a fitted line: it is the share of the total variance that sits between the targets being measured, against the share that sits within them.

That framing is what makes it read naturally as an agreement number. An ICC near $1$ means almost all the spread in the data comes from real, stable differences between the people or objects being rated; an ICC near $0$ means the ratings a single person or object receives vary about as much as the ratings different people or objects receive, so whatever produced the number was not tracking the thing it was supposedly rating.

There is a real trap hiding in how many forms it takes. Depending on the design, whether raters are the same set every time or a different random set, whether the interest is in absolute agreement or merely in consistent ordering, and whether one rating or an average of several is being reported, there are ten recognised forms of ICC, and they can give different numbers from the identical data. Stating which form is meant is not a formality; it changes the answer.
concepts.here: The dataset's origin used ICC to ask whether different visitors, looking at the same painting, reported the same emotion, and found inter-rater agreement near zero, the highest value $0.064$: the response came from the person, not the picture. This project instead reports Spearman correlation as a proxy for physiology-annotation alignment, since a true ICC needs shared-stimulus windows across visitors that are not yet linked in this pipeline, and pushes the same underlying question further with the crossed mixed-effects variance decomposition of Experiment 4, which splits the ratings themselves into a person share, a painting share and a residual on the same logic ICC is built from.
concepts.example: Suppose each of five paintings is rated once by each of several visitors. If most of the spread in all those ratings comes from some paintings being rated consistently higher than others, ICC sits close to $1$. If instead the ratings for any one painting bounce around almost as widely as the ratings across every painting put together, so that knowing which painting was rated barely narrows down the rating at all, ICC sits close to $0$, which is the pattern van der Kaaden found.
pitfalls: An ICC of $0.064$ is not "6% agreement" in any everyday sense; it says almost none of the spread in ratings is explained by which painting was viewed, with nearly all of it sitting in how one visitor differed from another.

The wrong ICC form for the design, agreement versus consistency, single measure versus an average of several, gives a different number from identical data; state the form before quoting a value, and do not compare two ICCs computed under different forms.

concepts.one_line: Building a fair null comparison for a time series by rotating it in a circle rather than scrambling it, so the fake version keeps every real property of the signal except its alignment with whatever it is being compared to.
concepts.explain:
Shuffling a time series row by row to build a "nothing going on" baseline is tempting but wrong for a signal like a per-second rating: it destroys the series' own autocorrelation, the fact that a rating this second is a good predictor of the rating next second, along with whatever real relationship is being tested. A shuffled null is therefore too weak. It makes a real signal's own smoothness look like evidence of a relationship that is not there, because a shuffled series loses that smoothness and any correlation against it looks large by comparison.

A circular shift avoids the problem by rotating the whole series by a random offset instead of scrambling it: whatever was at the end wraps around to the start. Every local property of the series, its autocorrelation, its overall shape, how much of it there is, survives completely intact. The only thing destroyed is the alignment between this series and whatever it is being compared against, since the two are now offset by an arbitrary, unrelated amount.

Repeating the shift many times and recomputing the statistic of interest each time builds a null distribution against which the real, unshifted alignment can be judged: if the real alignment's statistic sits comfortably inside the spread the random rotations already produce, there is nothing to explain beyond what the series' own smoothness would produce on its own.
concepts.here: This project's painting-level analysis (`scripts/painting_analysis/sharpening_null_check.py`) uses exactly this test to check whether scoping prediction to the attended painting genuinely strengthens the sensor-affect relationship, or only looks stronger because the row count drops when the whole session is narrowed to one painting. Within each participant, the affect axis is circularly shifted by a random offset, which preserves that participant's own autocorrelation and row count while destroying the alignment with the sensor features, and this is repeated 200 times to build a null for how much the relationship would appear to sharpen by chance alone. In one run of that check, all six condition-by-axis cells came back with the observed sharpening inside that null band (observed factors of $1.09$ to $1.85$ against null means of $1.05$ to $1.94$, $p=0.375$ to $0.685$), consistent with this thesis's broader finding that restricting the rows moves scores less than it first appears to.
concepts.example: A participant's arousal trace runs for 400 seconds. A circular shift by, say, 137 seconds moves second 400 to sit where second 263 used to be, second 1 to sit where second 138 used to be, and so on all the way around; nothing about how smoothly the trace itself moves has changed, but it is now compared against a completely different, unrelated stretch of the sensor features.
pitfalls: A row-shuffled null is not a substitute for a circular-shift null on autocorrelated data; the shuffled version is too weak and will make ordinary smoothness look like a real effect.

The shift has to be applied per participant, not across the whole pooled series at once, or a shift near a participant boundary would splice together two different people's data rather than rotating one person's own trace.

concepts.one_line: Building a confidence interval by rebuilding the dataset from its own rows, drawn with replacement, over and over, and reading the interval off how much a statistic wobbles across those rebuilds, instead of trusting a textbook formula for its uncertainty.
concepts.explain:
Some statistics have a clean textbook formula for how uncertain they are. Others, a variance share estimated from just five paintings, do not, or the formula that exists needs assumptions this data cannot promise to meet. The bootstrap sidesteps needing a formula at all: it resamples the actual collected data with replacement many times over, recomputing the statistic on each resample, and the spread across those recomputed values stands in for the uncertainty a formula would otherwise have to derive.

"With replacement" is the detail that makes it work: a resample can include the same visitor twice and leave another out entirely. That is deliberate. It mimics the real source of uncertainty in the study, which is that this particular set of visitors is only one of many cohorts that could have been recruited, and a resample stands in for one of those alternate cohorts.

What gets resampled matters as much as how. Rows from the same visitor are not independent draws of anything, exactly the concern behind the within-participant-correlation and Simpson's-paradox entries, so a valid bootstrap for a per-visitor quantity has to resample whole visitors, keeping every one of a chosen visitor's rows together, never individual rows in isolation.
concepts.here: A participant-level bootstrap is one of three checks placed around the painting-shared variance estimate, alongside a leave-one-painting-out refit and an eta-squared cross-check, because with only five paintings that estimate rests on the fewest independent units of the three components the variance decomposition produces. The protocol chapter also pairs a bootstrap confidence interval with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test whenever one setting is judged against another, throughout the thesis.
concepts.example: To put a confidence interval on the painting share from 46 participants, resample 46 participant-visits with replacement, so some visitors appear twice and others not at all, refit the crossed mixed-effects model on that resample, and record the painting share it produces. Repeating this a thousand times and reading off the middle 90% of the thousand recorded shares gives the interval.
pitfalls: Resampling individual rows instead of whole visitors quietly reintroduces the pooling problem this thesis works hard everywhere else to avoid, since two rows from the same visitor are not independent.

With only five paintings, no amount of participant resampling manufactures more paintings than were collected; the bootstrap widens the visible uncertainty around the painting share honestly, it cannot shrink the real limitation of having five units to estimate from.

concepts.term: Electrodermal activity: tonic level and phasic responses
concepts.one_line: Skin conductance carries two signals braided together: a slow floor that drifts over minutes with general arousal and skin contact, and fast, brief blips that mark a specific arousing moment within a couple of seconds.
concepts.explain:
Sweat glands are switched on by the sympathetic nervous system, the body's accelerating branch, and sweat makes skin a slightly better conductor of a tiny applied current. Skin conductance rises, in other words, when that branch is active. But the rise it produces is not one smooth thing; two distinct behaviours are braided together in the same recorded trace.

The tonic level is the slow-moving floor the signal keeps returning to, drifting up and down over tens of seconds to minutes as general arousal, skin temperature, or electrode contact changes. Riding on top of it are phasic skin-conductance responses: brief rises of a few tenths of a microsiemens that begin one to three seconds after a triggering event and decay again over the following few seconds, each one a candidate marker of a reaction to a specific moment.

Because both ride on the identical recorded trace, most of what "processing EDA" means in practice is separating the two cleanly, the tonic level for a slow trend, the phasic responses for reactivity to a specific stimulus, before either is handed to a downstream model. How that separation is actually done is a modelling choice in its own right (see the decomposition entry).
concepts.here: \ac{EDA} is decomposed into a tonic level and phasic responses for every recording, with the tonic level's mean, standard deviation and slope, and the phasic responses' count, mean, median and standard deviation of amplitude, and mean and median rise time, all carried forward as features. On the 25 raw recordings that pass quality checks and also carry a temperature channel, the tonic level rises and falls with skin temperature at a median Spearman $r=0.89$ across the visit, while the phasic responses show no such relationship at all (median $0.00$), which is exactly the tonic-versus-phasic split behaving as it should: one component absorbing warmth and contact, the other staying clean of it.
concepts.example: A visitor's tonic level might drift from $2.1$ to $2.4\,\mu S$ over ten minutes as the headset warms against their skin. Three seconds after a striking detail in a painting catches their eye, a distinct $0.15\,\mu S$ bump rises and decays within about five seconds on top of that drift, and it is the bump, not the drift, that a moment-specific analysis is actually looking for.
pitfalls: The tonic level partly measures skin temperature and electrode contact, not affect alone; in this cohort it tracks temperature at a median $r=0.89$, so a rising tonic level is a weak and confounded arousal cue on its own.

The smallest deflection conventionally counted as a real response is $0.01$ to $0.05\,\mu S$; a recording whose entire range barely clears that (this project's own flatness check removes anything spanning under $0.02\,\mu S$ between its 5th and 95th percentiles) is unusable rather than merely noisy.

concepts.term: EDA decomposition: convex optimisation versus filter-based
concepts.one_line: Two different ways to pull the slow tonic level and the fast phasic responses apart from one skin-conductance trace: one simply filters the signal into a slow and a fast band, the other solves a single optimisation problem that fits both parts to a physiological model of how a sweat response actually rises and falls.
concepts.explain:
The simplest separation is a frequency split: a low-pass filter tracks the slow tonic trend, and whatever is left over after subtracting it is called phasic. This is cheap, but it carries no notion of what a real phasic response is shaped like, so it cannot tell a genuine event apart from ordinary drift or noise sitting at a similar frequency, and it can just as easily invent a response that was not there or slice one real response into several.

The convex-optimisation approach instead models the observed trace as the sum of three things at once: a slowly varying tonic level, a phasic component built by convolving a known impulse shape with a sparse train of driver pulses, one pulse per real physiological event, and noise. Solving for the tonic level, the pulse train and the noise together, as one convex optimisation problem, guarantees a single global solution rather than one that depends on where the fitting happened to start, and because it builds in the shape a real response should have, it can separate two responses that overlap in time, which a frequency split cannot do at all.

Neither wins outright. An independent seven-method comparison found no approach universally best across datasets, which is exactly why this thesis treats the choice as something to search on its own data rather than assume.
concepts.here: Because no decomposition method is universally preferred, this thesis searches between the frequency-split and convex-optimisation (cvxEDA) decompositions, crossed with motion-mask multipliers of two, three and five median absolute deviations. NeuroKit2's implementation, under the five-deviation mask and a three-second window, is the configuration carried forward, but the sweep behind that choice found no candidate parameter, including this one, moving mean CCC by more than $0.016$: the two decomposition methods are read as tied on this cohort, not as one being shown to work better.
concepts.example: Given one skin-conductance trace with two real events three seconds apart, a frequency split can smear them into one broad bump or, depending on the filter's cutoff, chop one genuine event into two spurious ones. The convex-optimisation approach instead fits a driver pulse for each event against the known shape a response should have, and can recover both as separate events precisely because it knows what one response looks like rather than only what frequency band it should sit in.
pitfalls: The decomposition is a modelling choice, not a direct measurement; two decompositions of the identical raw trace can disagree about how many responses occurred and how large each one was.

In this project's own sweep, the choice of decomposition method changed almost nothing (no candidate here moved mean CCC by more than $0.016$), so a claim resting on one specific decomposition method being better than the other is not supported by anything found in this cohort.

concepts.one_line: Heart-rate variability measures the second-to-second timing of the heart's own electrical trigger, but a wrist sensor never sees that trigger; it sees the pulse of blood arriving afterwards, a close but not identical stand-in the field calls pulse-rate variability.
concepts.explain:
A heart at rest does not beat perfectly regularly, and the tiny variation in the timing between one beat and the next carries information about the balance between the body's accelerating and calming nervous-system branches. Properly measured, that is heart-rate variability, read from an ECG's electrical trace, which marks the exact instant each beat's electrical trigger fires.

A wrist-worn optical sensor sees none of that directly. It shines light into the skin and measures the rhythmic change in how much of it bounces back as blood volume rises and falls with each heartbeat, and that pulse of blood arrives a fraction of a second after the electrical trigger that caused it, with its own added jitter from the trip down the arm. The timing pattern recovered this way is close to, but not identical with, true cardiac HRV, and the field's own name for it is pulse-rate variability.

The indices computed from either signal fall into families. SDNN is the spread of every interval's length, a measure of total variation. RMSSD looks instead at how much each interval differs from the one right before it, which makes it especially sensitive to the fast, parasympathetic ("rest and digest") contribution, and valid even from a very short recording. The frequency bands split the same variability by how fast it oscillates: high-frequency power tracks fast, breathing-linked swings, while the low- and very-low-frequency bands need at least two and five minutes of clean recording respectively before they can be resolved at all. Poincar\'e-plot indices read the identical variability geometrically, by plotting each interval against the one immediately before it.

The gap between HRV and its pulse-based surrogate widens further under exactly the condition this thesis collects in: walking, rather than sitting still.
concepts.here: This thesis states the distinction plainly: "what an optical sensor yields is strictly pulse-rate variability, a surrogate for HRV." Beats are located with a detector validated at $99.8\%$ sensitivity on resting and post-exercise fingertip recordings, a validation that does not cover walking. Of 23 common HRV indices that stay valid at the sixty-second window this thesis uses, four are kept, meanNN, SDNN, RMSSD, high-frequency power, and Poincar\'e SD2, while the low- and very-low-frequency bands are excluded outright for needing longer records than a museum visit's windows provide.
concepts.example: For four consecutive intervals of $800, 820, 780, 830$ ms, the successive differences are $+20, -40, +50$ ms; squaring and averaging those three gives $1500\,\text{ms}^2$, and its square root, about $38.7$ ms, is the RMSSD, a single number summarising how much the heartbeat's timing jittered from one beat to the next.
pitfalls: A wrist-PPG RMSSD or SDNN is not literally "HRV" in the ECG-validated sense; treat it as a related but imperfect surrogate, and a worse one still during movement.

The low- and very-low-frequency HRV bands need at least two and five minutes of clean recording to resolve at all; computing them over a sixty-second window would be meaningless, which is exactly why this thesis excludes them rather than reports them unreliably.

concepts.one_line: A cheap way to see the pulse of blood under the skin by shining light and measuring how much bounces back, which works beautifully at rest and degrades badly the moment a wrist starts moving.
concepts.explain:
An LED shines into the skin and a photodetector measures the light that returns. Blood volume under the skin rises and falls with every heartbeat, which changes how much light gets absorbed on the way, and that rhythmic change, one peak per heartbeat, is the photoplethysmography (PPG) waveform: a way to estimate heart rate cheaply, with no electrodes, from a wristband or a fingertip clip.

The sensor cannot tell a light change caused by blood volume apart from a light change caused by anything else moving between the LED, the skin and the detector. Walking moves the wrist, which moves the sensor against the skin, and that motion can swamp the real pulse signal, adding beats that never happened, deleting ones that did, or shifting them in time. The multi-step cleaning this thesis applies, locating beats, then filtering out intervals whose difference from their neighbour exceeds a bound (see the HRV entry), exists specifically to catch and repair exactly this kind of damage. The field's usual remedy, an accelerometer as a motion reference for cleaning the trace, is not applied on this channel here; instead, every window carries its own record of how much of it needed repair and how much of it coincided with detected motion, so a contaminated stretch stays visible to the model rather than silently trusted.
concepts.here: The wristband writes a BVP sample exactly $64$ times per second in every recording, so nothing about the timing of the raw signal can be wrong, only the values it carries. Beat detection is validated at $99.8\%$ sensitivity on resting and post-exercise fingertip recordings, a validation that does not extend to walking, which is most of what this dataset contains. Three visitors, M18, M26 and M37, have no usable BVP recording at all, and of these, M18 (rcea) and M37 (retro) fall inside the analysed streams and carry no valid HRV feature as a result.
concepts.example: A visitor swings an arm while walking between paintings. The sensor's light path against the skin flexes with every stride, and for a few seconds the detected "beats" arrive roughly twice as often as the heart is actually beating, an artefact the successive-difference filter is built to catch and interpolate over rather than trust as real cardiac activity.
pitfalls: A PPG trace collected during movement can look like a perfectly plausible heartbeat signal while being mostly motion artefact; a fixed sampling rate guarantees nothing about whether the values themselves are trustworthy.

Two participants in this dataset have no usable BVP recording at all; any HRV feature for them is missing outright, not merely degraded, and is imputed like any other missing feature rather than estimated from a bad signal.

concepts.one_line: Reading the pupil's own size as a signal, on the idea that it widens not only for light but for mental effort and emotional arousal, so a change in diameter can mark a moment of processing even when nothing about the room got darker.
concepts.explain:
The pupil's job is to control how much light reaches the retina, but the muscles that resize it are wired into the same nervous-system pathways that arousal and cognitive load also drive. Pupillometry is the practice of reading pupil diameter over time on that basis: a reliable, non-light-driven change in diameter, a task-evoked response, is taken as evidence of something happening in the mind rather than in the eye.

What is known is that pupil size grows with arousal and dilates to both pleasant and unpleasant stimuli relative to neutral ones, which means the direction of a widening pupil says little about whether the moment felt good or bad, only that something notable happened. The complication that shadows the whole practice is that light is a vastly stronger driver of pupil size than any cognitive or emotional cause, so most of what makes pupillometry rigorous is controlling for, or explicitly modelling, light before trusting anything else the pupil seems to say.

A standard cleaning chain exists precisely because the raw diameter trace is noisy and confounded: discard samples the tracker itself flags as invalid or physiologically implausible, average the two eyes together, bridge short blink-induced gaps by interpolation, and remove the pupil's own slow drift with a rolling baseline before treating any remaining movement as a candidate signal.
concepts.here: Diameters outside $1.5$ to $9.0$\,mm are discarded, gaps shorter than half a second are bridged by interpolation, and a rolling 30-second mean is subtracted as a baseline. The two eyes' diameters agree at a median $r=0.92$ across the cohort, with one exception (M38, $r=0.12$) kept rather than dropped. This dataset carries no luminance channel at all, so the light confound that pupillometry guidelines ask studies to report or control can only be stated here, never removed.
concepts.example: A visitor's pupil might widen briefly on turning to face a painting, purely because the wall behind it is darker than the corridor they just left. A second, smaller widening a moment later, while looking at the same patch of the same painting under the same light, is the kind of change pupillometry is actually trying to isolate, and this dataset cannot fully tell the two apart because it has no record of scene luminance at all.
pitfalls: Luminance changes the pupil far more than emotion or effort does; without a luminance channel, any pupil-arousal relationship reported here is confounded by whatever the visitor happened to be looking at.

Pupil size also responds to mental effort and to viewing distance, not to affect alone, so a change in diameter is evidence that something happened, not proof of which emotion, or even that an emotion, caused it.

concepts.term: Pupil foreshortening error and baseline correction
concepts.one_line: A pupil viewed at an angle looks smaller than it really is, purely as a matter of geometry, and that shrinkage can be as large as the genuine cognitive or emotional change the pupil is being measured for.
concepts.explain:
An eye tracker's camera photographs the pupil from one fixed position. When the eye rotates to look off to the side, the camera now sees the pupil's circular opening from an angle rather than straight on, and any circle photographed edge-on measures narrower across than it really is, exactly the way a coin held flat looks like an ellipse rather than a circle once tilted. The pupil has not physically changed size at all; the camera's view of it has. This is pupil foreshortening error, and in head-mounted trackers its size can rival the very responses pupillometry is trying to detect, with gaze position alone accounting for $9\%$ to $20\%$ of measured pupil variance depending on the tracker.

A separate but related idea is baseline correction. Even once foreshortening is handled, a pupil's absolute diameter at any moment reflects wherever it happened to already be, not only what just happened to it. Baseline correction removes a reference level, measured just before the moment of interest, so what remains is the change caused by that moment rather than the level the pupil started from. The standard treatment subtracts that reference rather than dividing by it, since subtraction behaves better when diameters are small or noisy.

Both corrections exist to strip away something real but uninteresting, geometry in one case, starting level in the other, so that what is left over is closer to whatever the pupil is actually being asked to reveal.
concepts.here: The correction this thesis tests regresses each participant's diameter on their own gaze direction and keeps the residual, a direct test of whether the correction helps in a headset rather than an assumption that it must. Because a free-roaming visit has no fixed trial onset to lock a baseline to, the reference level used throughout is a rolling 30-second mean, subtracted from the raw diameter, rather than a single pre-trial baseline. Gaze-angle correction was one of the five searched configuration parameters, and it did not separate from leaving the diameter uncorrected: the uncorrected diameter was carried forward at the selection resolution, as a tie resolved toward the simpler option, not as a demonstrated advantage.
concepts.example: A visitor looks straight ahead at a painting and then glances toward its text panel thirty degrees to the side. The measured pupil diameter can shrink noticeably at that angle purely from foreshortening, even if the true pupil and the visitor's arousal have not changed at all; the gaze-angle correction is meant to remove exactly that shrinkage before anything about the remaining change is read as a signal.
pitfalls: A pupil that looks smaller while a visitor glances toward the edge of a scene may only be foreshortened, not less aroused; check the gaze angle at that moment before reading a diameter drop as an affect signal.

This project's own sweep found gaze-angle correction and no correction tied at the selection resolution, so carrying the uncorrected diameter forward reflects a tie broken toward simplicity on this cohort, not evidence that the correction is unhelpful in general.

sources.title: Hayes and Petrov (2016), Mapping and correcting the influence of gaze position on pupil size measurements
Petersch and Dierkes (2022), Gaze-angle dependency of pupil-size measurements in head-mounted eye tracking

concepts.one_line: Deciding, sample by sample, whether the eye was resting on a point (a fixation) or flicking rapidly between points (a saccade), a call made almost entirely from how fast the gaze was moving or how tightly it clustered, and one that different rules can make differently on the identical recording.
concepts.explain:
A raw eye-tracker stream is just a sequence of gaze directions over time. A fixation is a spell where gaze holds roughly still, the moments visual and cognitive processing actually happen; a saccade is the rapid flick between such spells, during which almost nothing useful is perceived. Almost every downstream eye-movement feature, fixation duration, saccade rate, depends on first telling the two apart.

Three families of rule do this differently. A velocity threshold classifies each sample by how fast the gaze is currently moving, above a cutoff is a saccade. A dispersion rule instead looks at how tightly a short window of samples clusters in space, tight clustering means a fixation regardless of speed. An adaptive rule estimates its own threshold from the recording itself, iteratively, rather than fixing one value in advance, so a noisier recording earns a more forgiving cutoff automatically rather than misclassifying its extra noise as eye movement.

The right cutoff genuinely depends on context, not just on which family is chosen. Thirty degrees per second is the standard velocity threshold for seated, screen-based viewing, but walking introduces its own eye-stabilising movements that a 30-degree threshold reads as constant saccading, which is why 240 degrees per second is validated specifically for walking instead. A dispersion rule calibrated on this exact headset class also exists, though only from a stationary task.
concepts.here: Four candidate rules, spanning the velocity-threshold, dispersion, and adaptive families, are compared on this cohort, starting from a 30-degrees-per-second velocity threshold as the default. The largest difference any of the five searched configuration parameters produced anywhere in Experiment 1 was $0.036$ mean CCC, and the fixation rule was not the parameter that produced it; no rule here separated from the others by more than the $0.08$ selection resolution, so the 30-degrees-per-second rule is carried forward as the simplest tied candidate, not as the one shown to work best in a free-roaming visit.
concepts.example: A visitor's gaze crosses from a painting to its text panel in 80 ms, covering a wide angle very fast, comfortably over even the 240-degree-per-second walking threshold, and every rule agrees that stretch is a saccade. A slower drift across the same distance while the visitor is simultaneously walking could be called a fixation by the 30-degree seated threshold and a saccade by the 240-degree walking one, from the identical raw samples.
pitfalls: A fixation rule tuned for seated, screen-based viewing (30 degrees per second) can misclassify ordinary walking-induced eye movement as a stream of saccades; check which setting a rule was validated for before trusting it in a free-roaming visit.

This project's own comparison could not tell the four rules apart (no more than $0.036$ mean CCC difference against a resolution of $0.08$), so carrying the 30-degree rule forward is a tie resolved toward the most established option, not a demonstrated advantage.

Nyström and Holmqvist (2010), An adaptive algorithm for fixation, saccade, and glissade detection in eyetracking data
Llanes-Jurado et al. (2020), Development and calibration of an eye-tracking fixation identification algorithm for immersive virtual reality

aka: extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set
concepts.one_line: A standardised list of 88 numbers, mostly about pitch, loudness and voice quality, chosen by a committee of speech researchers specifically because they carry emotional information and generalise across studies, rather than a list every lab invents for itself.
concepts.explain:
Speech carries affect not only in the words spoken but in how they are spoken: pitch rising, a voice trembling, speech speeding up, volume dropping. Turning a raw recording into numbers a model can use means deciding exactly which acoustic properties to measure, and for a long time every speech-emotion study effectively invented its own list, which made results from different studies hard to compare or trust.

GeMAPS, and its extended version eGeMAPS with 88 parameters, was assembled by a committee of speech and affective-computing researchers specifically to end that fragmentation. The parameters were chosen for a known link to how voice is physically produced, loudness, pitch and its variability, the formant frequencies that shape vowel quality, jitter and shimmer that capture roughness in the voice, spectral balance, and the set is deliberately kept small rather than exhaustive, to guard against over-fitting a modest dataset with hundreds of barely-used features.

Because the set is standardised, it is aggregated over the unit it was defined for, one utterance, rather than over an arbitrary fixed window, which is what lets it be compared meaningfully across studies that never shared a single line of code.
concepts.here: This thesis computes all 88 eGeMAPS parameters with openSMILE, aggregated per utterance, "because the utterance is the unit for which the standardised acoustic set is defined." Across the 176 tests this produces per stream (88 parameters times two axes), the median absolute Spearman correlation against the ratings is $0.03$ on rcea and $0.07$ on retro, with four and five tests respectively reaching $p<0.05$ before correction and none surviving it.
concepts.example: Two of the 88 parameters are the mean pitch, in semitones relative to a reference, and the local jitter, a measure of cycle-to-cycle instability in that pitch. A visitor's voice rising in pitch and becoming slightly less steady while describing a painting would move both of these numbers, independently of whatever words were actually said.
pitfalls: The 88 parameters need a usable utterance to exist at all; speech covers a median of only $6.9\%$ of a visitor's analysed seconds, so eGeMAPS features are missing for the great majority of rows in this dataset, routinely rather than exceptionally.

A parameter set built for how something is spoken says nothing about what was said; VADER sentiment covers that separately, and the two are counted as different sensors in this thesis precisely because they answer different questions about the same recording.

sources.title: Eyben et al. (2016), The Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set (GeMAPS) for voice research and affective computing

aka: Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner
concepts.one_line: A training-free way to score how positive or negative a piece of text sounds, built from a hand-checked dictionary of words and a handful of grammar rules, rather than a model that had to learn from labelled examples of its own.
concepts.explain:
A machine-learned sentiment classifier needs its own labelled training set, sentences someone has already scored, before it can score anything new. A lexicon-based scorer sidesteps that entirely: it starts from a large list of words that people have independently rated for how positive or negative they feel, "great" strongly positive, "terrible" strongly negative, "the" neutral, and scores a piece of text mostly by looking its words up in that list. With no model to train, it can be applied to a brand-new corpus immediately, with no risk of quietly overfitting to whatever this project's own cohort happened to say.

What makes VADER specifically suited to this setting is what it was built and validated on: short, informal, social-media-style text, closer to an off-the-cuff spoken remark to a museum guide than to edited, formal prose. It also layers a handful of grammatical rules on top of the raw word list, an intensifier like "very" strengthens the following word's score, a negation like "not" flips it, so it reads a little more like a person weighing a sentence than a bare word count would.

The honest limit is the gap between what VADER was validated on and what it is asked to score here: written social-media text, not speech transcribed automatically from a live conversation, which carries its own recognition errors and off-the-cuff phrasing that written posts do not. Treating that transfer as safe is an assumption this thesis states rather than tests.
concepts.here: Speech content is scored per utterance with the VADER lexicon, producing "one compound sentiment score" as speech content's entire feature set, the smallest of any sensor in this thesis. Against the ratings, it manages a median absolute correlation of $0.04$ on rcea and $0.06$ on retro across only two tests per stream (one score against two axes), with none reaching significance.
concepts.example: A transcribed remark like "this one is really beautiful" scores strongly positive, since "beautiful" carries a high positive value in the lexicon and "really", an intensifier, pushes the score higher still. A flatter description like "this is a painting of a woman" scores close to neutral, since none of its words carry a strong charge in the lexicon either way.
pitfalls: VADER was validated on written social-media text, not spoken and transcribed remarks; an automatic transcription's own errors, a mis-heard word, a dropped negation, can flip a sentiment score for reasons that have nothing to do with what the visitor actually felt.

Like every speech feature in this thesis, VADER's score exists only for the seconds an utterance covers, a small minority of any visit, so it is missing for most rows rather than merely noisy on them.

sources.title: Hutto and Gilbert (2014), VADER: A parsimonious rule-based model for sentiment analysis of social media text

concepts.one_line: Stretching and compressing one time series' own clock, locally, until it lines up with another's shape as closely as possible, then reporting only how much disagreement is left over once that best possible stretching has been applied.
concepts.explain:
Two recordings of a related process rarely move in lockstep, even when they are genuinely related: one lags the other, or speeds up and slows down relative to it. Comparing them second-for-second, by raw timestamp, can line up a rising stretch in one series against a falling stretch in the other purely because they happened to occur at the same clock time, not because the two series actually disagree in shape.

Dynamic time warping instead finds a warping path: a fine-grained mapping of one series' points onto the other's, stretching or compressing the timeline in either direction wherever doing so brings the shapes into closer alignment, without touching the recorded values themselves at all. The path must move forward in both series and cover both endpoints, so it can stretch the gaps between events but never reorder the events themselves, and it is found by dynamic programming, building up the best cumulative cost to every point from the best cost to the points just before it.

What DTW hands back is a single number, not a repaired signal: the distance still separating the two series once the best possible warp has been applied, normalised by the length of the path that achieved it. That number is a similarity score for the shapes, and it is most meaningful when the warping is kept close to the diagonal, a slope constraint, since a warp left entirely free can be stretched enough to make almost any two series look alike.
concepts.here: This thesis uses DTW as one of four representation-level alignment methods compared in Experiment 2, adding three columns for each of three sensor pairs, pupil-EDA, pupil-HRV, EDA-HRV: the leftover warped distance, the mean signed offset along the path in $0.25$-second grid samples, and how far the path departs from the diagonal. Both signals of a pair are read from a shared twelve-second trailing window on a 4 Hz grid and standardised before warping. Its mean CCC across the four slices, $+0.0177$, is the lowest of the four alignment arms compared, against $+0.0199$ for fixed windowing, $+0.0236$ for DCCA and $+0.0179$ for DCTW, though the entire $0.006$ spread between all four sits far inside the $0.08$ selection resolution, so none is shown to beat the others; the warped block is also missing on an eighth of the retro rows, thinning DTW further in the two slices where it already scores lowest.
concepts.example: Two similarly shaped bumps in two different signals peak two seconds apart. Read off a fixed, unwarped window, they look like a poor match, since one is rising exactly where the other is already falling. DTW recognises the same underlying shape by locally stretching one series' timeline until its bump's peak slides onto the other's, and reports a small leftover distance once that stretch is applied.
pitfalls: DTW's output is a distance, not an aligned pair of signals; it cannot be fed into a model as a repaired version of either sensor, only as a feature summarising how well the two matched once warped.

An unconstrained warp can force almost any two series to resemble each other, since it is free to stretch time arbitrarily; the original work itself found DTW discriminates best under a slope constraint, and treating an unconstrained warp's low distance as strong evidence of a real relationship overstates what was actually found.
