concepts.term: Canonical correlation analysis, and its deep version
concepts.one_line: Finding one weighted combination of each sensor's own features such that the two combinations correlate with each other as strongly as possible, rather than correlating any one feature from one sensor against any one feature from the other.
concepts.explain:
Two sensors rarely have a single feature from each that lines up neatly with a single feature from the other. What usually happens instead is that some combination of several features from one sensor tracks some combination of several features from the other, and no individual pairwise correlation shows it. Canonical correlation analysis is built to find exactly that: a weighted sum of one view's features and a weighted sum of the other's, chosen jointly so that the two resulting sums correlate as strongly as two single numbers possibly can.

The classical version can only find combinations that are linear, a straight weighted sum, of the original features. Deep canonical correlation analysis (DCCA) replaces that straight sum with a neural network on each side, so the two views are each transformed through a learned nonlinear function before their correlation is maximised, capturing relationships a linear combination cannot express.

CCA and DCCA perform no warping of time at all; the two views are assumed to already sit on the same clock, one column of one lined up with one column of the other. That is also their most restrictive requirement: because the objective is built on the cross-covariance between the two views, they need genuinely paired observations, and the method as originally proposed handles views recorded at different rates by downsampling the faster one down to the slower one's rate, discarding whatever the faster view offered above that.
concepts.here: \ac{DCCA} is one of the four representation-level alignment methods this thesis compares in Experiment 2, adding learned correlated projections for each of the three sensor pairs, fitted inside each outer training fold on the training participants alone and applied unchanged to the held-out visitor. Its mean CCC across the four slices, $+0.0236$, is the highest of the four alignment arms, ahead of fixed windowing's $+0.0199$ by about $0.004$, a twentieth of the $0.08$ selection resolution, so nothing in this comparison shows that projecting the sensor pairs into a correlated space actually helps; DCCA is read as tied with the others, not as the winner its raw ranking suggests.
concepts.example: Pupil diameter and skin conductance might each carry several features, none individually correlated with the other sensor's individual features. CCA can still find that, say, a specific mix of diameter mean and dilation slope on one side correlates at $0.6$ with a specific mix of tonic level and response count on the other, a relationship invisible to any single feature-pair correlation.
pitfalls: CCA and DCCA assume the two views are already aligned in time; if a real lag exists between two sensors, neither method corrects for it, since maximising correlation between mismatched-in-time views only papers over a timing problem rather than solving it.

DCCA is fitted fresh inside every training fold in this thesis specifically so the held-out visitor never shapes the learned projection; a version fitted once on the whole cohort and reused across folds would leak that visitor's own data into the alignment step.

sources.title: Andrew et al. (2013), Deep canonical correlation analysis
scikit-learn, CCA (canonical correlation analysis)

concepts.one_line: Learning new features for two sensors and a warping of their shared timeline at once, so the transformed signals end up both maximally correlated and lined up in time, instead of assuming one of those two problems is already solved before tackling the other.
concepts.explain:
Dynamic time warping (its own entry) can stretch a timeline but never changes what the features themselves mean. Deep canonical correlation analysis (also its own entry) can learn new, more informative features but assumes the two views are already sitting on the same clock. Deep canonical time warping asks for both at once: it learns a nonlinear transformation of each sensor's features, the DCCA half, while simultaneously warping the timeline the way DTW does, so that the transformed signals come out both temporally aligned and as correlated as the learned features can make them.

Because the two problems, what the features should be and how the timeline should bend, depend on each other, DCTW does not solve them in one step. It alternates: hold the current warping fixed and improve the feature transformation, then hold that transformation fixed and improve the warping, back and forth until neither step improves things further. That alternation is also its main practical cost, since each of the two halves is itself an optimisation problem, run repeatedly rather than once.
concepts.here: \ac{DCTW} is one of the four alignment methods compared in Experiment 2, adding a warping step on top of the same learned projections DCCA produces for each of the three sensor pairs, fitted inside each outer training fold on the training participants alone. Its mean CCC across the four slices, $+0.0179$, sits just above DTW's $+0.0177$ and below both fixed windowing ($+0.0199$) and DCCA ($+0.0236$), all four within the $0.08$ selection resolution of one another, so adding a learned warp on top of a learned projection is not shown to help beyond what the simpler alternatives already achieve on this cohort.
concepts.example: Given a pupil signal and a skin-conductance signal that are both mismatched in timing and only weakly related feature-for-feature, DCTW can, in principle, discover a combination of pupil features that responds two seconds ahead of a combination of EDA features, learning the useful combination and the two-second offset together rather than being handed either one in advance.
pitfalls: Alternating between the warp and the projection can settle into a locally good but globally mediocre solution, since each half is optimised holding the other fixed rather than jointly; a different starting point can land somewhere else entirely.

The original DCTW experiments align sequences of several thousand samples with a network topology chosen to limit overfitting at that scale, and evaluate it on the same sequences it was fitted to; applying it to a small, held-out-participant protocol, as this thesis does, is a considerably harder setting than the one it was originally demonstrated on.

sources.title: Trigeorgis et al. (2016), Deep canonical time warping

concepts.one_line: Where several sensors are available, the question of how to combine them splits into three genuinely different choices: mix their raw features before modelling, mix each sensor's own separate prediction after modelling, or build one model whose internal structure is shaped around having several sensors from the start.
concepts.explain:
Early fusion concatenates every sensor's features into a single wide table and hands the whole thing to one model, so the model itself decides how much weight each modality gets, implicitly, through however it ends up using each column. It is the simplest option, and it lets the model discover interactions between sensors that neither could show alone, but it also means every sensor shares one set of hyperparameters and one training process, whether or not that suits all of them equally well.

Late fusion instead lets each sensor keep its own separate model, trained and tuned on that sensor's own features alone, and combines only the predictions that come out the far end, by a simple average, a weighted average, or a second model trained on top of the base predictions. Each sensor's pipeline stays independent, which makes it easy to add or drop a sensor without retraining everything else, and easy to see which sensor's own prediction is driving a given result.

Model-level fusion sits between the two: rather than concatenating raw features or combining finished predictions, it builds sensor-specific structure into one model itself, letting the modalities interact inside the model at some intermediate stage rather than only at the input or only at the output. It asks the most of the model's design, since that internal coupling has to be built for the specific application rather than reused off the shelf.

None of the three is universally superior; which one wins depends on how strongly the sensors interact, how much data is available to fit whatever the fusion step adds, and how important it is to keep each sensor's contribution legible on its own.
concepts.here: This thesis runs four combination mechanisms in Experiment 2 under this framework: early fusion (concatenating all five sensors' features into the standard model), early fusion with the cross-sensor block added, and two late-fusion variants, simple averaging and CCC-weighted averaging of each sensor's own Experiment 1 prediction. Model-level fusion, coupling the modalities inside the model's own internal structure, is discussed in the literature review but not run as a fifth arm, since every mechanism actually tested here is either fitting-free or a single fit of the standard model, keeping every arm on the identical protocol as Experiment 1.
pitfalls: Late fusion needs its own rule for a missing sensor, since it combines predictions rather than features; this thesis renormalises the averaging weights over whichever sensors did produce a prediction for a given row, rather than dropping the row.

CCC-weighted late fusion floors a sensor's weight at zero whenever its own CCC is negative; without that floor, a negative weight would invert that sensor's prediction rather than simply discount an unreliable one.

sources.title: Poria et al. (2017), A review of affective computing: from unimodal analysis to multimodal fusion

concepts.one_line: A feature that describes neither what one sensor did nor what another did, but whether the two moved together, which is information a model can only see if that relationship is measured and handed to it directly.
concepts.explain:
Placing two sensors on a shared timeline says nothing about how they actually move relative to each other. A model given the pupil diameter and the skin conductance level separately still has to discover, on its own, whether the two rise and fall together, whether one leads the other, or whether they are unrelated at that moment; nothing in either feature alone states it. A cross-sensor coupling feature computes that relationship directly and adds it as its own column, so the model receives "these two moved together" as a fact rather than having to infer it from two separate traces.

Such features can take several forms: a plain correlation between two signals over a window, a correlation allowed to shift one signal against the other before settling on the strongest match it finds, a count of how often an event in one signal is reliably followed by an event in the other, or a simple ratio between two signals' typical levels. What they share is that each measures a relationship, not a magnitude, and that relationship depends heavily on the window it is computed over: a multiverse analysis of one such measure found that window length alone shifted the size of the estimated coupling, how much it varied, and in one case even the direction of the effect being tested.

A closely related idea learns the coupling instead of measuring it directly, projecting two sensors into a shared space where they correlate as strongly as possible (see the canonical correlation analysis entry); keeping the measured and the learned versions separate is what lets each be judged on its own rather than one masquerading as evidence for the other.
concepts.here: This thesis adds nine such columns in Experiment 2, built on three 1 Hz signals rather than on the aggregated features of Experiment 1: the baseline-corrected pupil diameter, the phasic electrodermal component, and the instantaneous heart rate. Six are correlations (two per pair, one static and one allowed to shift by up to five seconds), two count how often a skin-conductance response follows a pupil dilation within three seconds, and one is a ratio between tonic pupil size and mean heart period. The window these are computed over is itself swept, between thirty and sixty seconds, rather than assumed, precisely because of the sensitivity the multiverse literature reports.
concepts.example: If a pupil dilation reliably precedes a skin-conductance response by about two seconds, a plain same-moment correlation between the two signals would miss that relationship almost entirely, since the two are rarely large at the identical instant. The shift-allowed correlation, and the explicit count of dilation-then-response events within a three-second window, are built specifically to catch a coupling like this one that a same-instant comparison would score as near zero.
pitfalls: The size, and sometimes even the direction, of a coupling estimate depends on the window length it is computed over; this thesis compares thirty- against sixty-second windows for exactly this reason rather than fixing one by convention.
A cross-sensor feature measures covariation, not causation; two signals moving together within a window does not establish which, if either, drove the other, only that they moved together.

concepts.term: Random forests and extremely randomised trees
concepts.one_line: Both build a large crowd of decision trees and average their predictions, but they disagree on how much randomness to force into growing each tree, and that one difference is what separates the two families.
concepts.explain:
A single decision tree splits the data again and again, each split chosen to best separate the outcome, until it reaches a prediction. Grown to its full depth, one tree fits its own training data closely and generalises poorly. A random forest tames this by growing many trees instead of one and averaging their predictions, and it forces each tree to differ from the others by training it on a random bootstrap resample of the rows and, at each split, only letting it choose the best cut among a random subset of the features rather than all of them. The averaging over many such deliberately-varied trees cancels out much of any single tree's overfitting.

Extremely randomised trees push the same idea further. Instead of searching for the best cut point among the randomly chosen candidate features at each split, as a random forest does, they pick the cut point at random too, and typically train each tree on the whole dataset rather than a bootstrap resample. That extra randomness raises the bias of any single tree slightly, but lowers the variance across the forest as a whole, and it is also considerably cheaper to compute, since it skips the search for the single best cut point at every split.

Which of the two wins is not settled in general and depends on the data. In this thesis, across eight model families compared on tabular sensor features from a small cohort, extremely randomised trees and CatBoost, another tree ensemble, tie for best.
concepts.here: Extremely randomised trees is the standard model this thesis carries into every experiment from Experiment 2 onward. Among the tree ensembles compared in Experiment 1, CatBoost's mean CCC across twenty cells, $+0.0062$, leads extremely randomised trees' $+0.0055$ by $0.0007$, a hundredth of the $0.08$ selection resolution, so the two are read as tied and the tie is resolved toward the family whose scores vary least across cells: extremely randomised trees at a standard deviation of $0.034$ against CatBoost's $0.043$. A random forest is also in the comparison, since it is one of the four families the dataset's origin used, and posts both the single highest cell of the whole experiment ($+0.119$) and the lowest mean of the eight families, illustrating how unstable any one tree family's ranking is at this cohort size.
concepts.example: Given the same twenty training rows, a random forest might grow one tree that first splits on tonic EDA level and another that first splits on pupil diameter, since each tree only sees a random subset of features at each split; extremely randomised trees goes further and might have both trees split on tonic EDA level but at two different, randomly chosen threshold values, rather than each tree searching for its own single best threshold.
pitfalls: Extremely randomised trees typically train each tree on the full dataset rather than a bootstrap resample, unlike a random forest; a comparison between the two that assumes both bootstrap identically is comparing configurations neither family actually uses by default.

In this thesis's own Experiment 1, the eight compared model families span only $0.0107$ mean CCC among their twenty-cell means, well inside the $0.08$ resolution, so extremely randomised trees being carried forward reflects a tied choice resolved toward stability, not a demonstrated advantage over CatBoost, ridge regression, or the other six families.

concepts.term: Variance decomposition into person, shared and residual parts
concepts.one_line: Splitting the total spread in a set of ratings into three separate shares, one that recurs whenever a specific stimulus reappears, one that stays constant for one person across every stimulus, and whatever is left over, before ever asking whether a model could predict any of it.
concepts.explain:
Any measured rating plausibly has three sources: something about the specific thing being rated, something stable about the specific person rating it, and everything else, moment-to-moment movement that fits neither category. A model trying to predict the rating for someone new can, at best, ever recover the part that recurs across the cohort. Knowing how the total variance actually splits three ways therefore sets, before any model is even built, a ceiling on what any model applied to that target could achieve.

The tool for this is a crossed random-intercepts mixed-effects model. "Crossed" means the person and the stimulus are treated as two separate, overlapping sources of variation, neither nested inside the other, since in principle every person can encounter every stimulus. It is fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML), a fitting method chosen specifically because it estimates variance components without the downward bias that plain maximum likelihood introduces when the number of groups involved is small. Each variance component, divided by the sum of all three, gives that source's share of the total.

A share is a partition of variance, not a measure of how different two people's average ratings are, and not a measure of agreement. A tiny stimulus share does not mean two stimuli barely differ in what they evoke; it means they differ little relative to how much people differ from each other and from their own moment-to-moment experience. Because a share this small rests on comparatively few independent stimulus units, it deserves more scrutiny than a single point estimate, not less: a bootstrap confidence interval, a leave-one-stimulus-out refit, and a cross-check by an entirely different route (an eta-squared variance ratio) are the natural guards to place around it.
concepts.here: This thesis fits exactly this model on the ratings themselves, with person and painting as the two crossed random intercepts, and finds that the share shared between visitors viewing the same painting sits at $0.0\%$ to $1.4\%$, against $36.6\%$ to $64.7\%$ carried by a stable difference between people; holding the painting fixed does not change this, since the painting-shared component stays at or below $2.6\%$ under either estimation method, and no individual sensor's own painting share, computed by the identical model applied to that sensor's features, exceeds $2.9\%$. Heart-rate variability is the most person-locked sensor of the five, at an $84.0\%$ to $84.3\%$ person share across slices. A fit whose person or painting component collapses below $0.05\%$ is recorded as degenerate and excluded from its category's mean, with the excluded count reported alongside.
concepts.example: Suppose three visitors each rate five paintings. If almost none of the spread across all fifteen ratings comes from which painting was shown, but each visitor has a consistently higher or lower average across all five paintings than the other two visitors, nearly all of the variance sits in the person component and almost none in the painting component, exactly the pattern this thesis reports at cohort scale.
pitfalls: A painting share near zero does not mean the paintings look indistinguishable; it means they explain little of the rating's variance next to how much people differ from each other and from their own moment-to-moment experience, a claim about variance shares, not about the paintings themselves.

A crossed model whose person or painting component collapses to its lower boundary has not actually divided the variance; the surviving component silently absorbs what the collapsed one should have carried, which is why this thesis flags and excludes any fit with a component under $0.05\%$ rather than reporting a share the model never really estimated.

concepts.term: Gradient boosting and its named implementations
concepts.one_line: Building one tree at a time, each new tree trained specifically to correct whatever the trees before it still get wrong, rather than growing many independent trees at once and averaging them the way a random forest does.
concepts.explain:
A random forest grows its trees independently and in parallel, then averages them. Gradient boosting grows trees in sequence instead: each new tree is fitted specifically to the error the ensemble so far still makes, so the model improves through a chain of small, targeted corrections rather than through many independent, unrelated guesses. Because each tree depends on the ones before it, boosting is inherently sequential, and its central risk is the opposite of a random forest's: too many rounds, or too little shrinkage on each tree's contribution, and the model starts correcting for noise rather than signal, which is why it is normally tuned with a learning rate that deliberately shrinks each new tree's effect.

XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and scikit-learn's own histogram-based gradient boosting are four engineering implementations of essentially the same underlying idea. They differ chiefly in how they build each tree efficiently, how continuous features get binned, how the best split is searched for, whether categorical features get special treatment, rather than in what boosting itself is doing conceptually. Running all four side by side is a way of asking whether the boosting idea helps at all, independent of any one library's particular tricks: if the choice of library changed the answer, that would say more about engineering than about the method.
concepts.here: "The four boosting entries are one method under four libraries, so the choice of library cannot decide the result." None of the four separates meaningfully from the rest of the eight model families compared in Experiment 1: CatBoost posts the highest mean CCC of all eight families ($+0.0062$) and wins four of twenty cells, while XGBoost ($+0.0039$), histogram gradient boosting ($+0.0017$) and LightGBM ($-0.0002$) all sit inside the same tie band, alongside ridge regression and the tree ensembles.
concepts.example: Given a first tree that predicts arousal reasonably well overall but systematically underestimates it whenever tonic EDA level is high, gradient boosting's next tree is trained specifically on that leftover underestimate, focused on exactly the pattern the first tree missed, rather than refitting the whole target from scratch the way an independent new tree in a random forest would.
pitfalls: More boosting rounds is not automatically better; each additional tree keeps chasing whatever error remains, including noise, so an unconstrained round count overfits the same way an unconstrained single tree's depth does.

Four different libraries agreeing with each other, as they do in this thesis, is evidence the boosting idea itself was tested fairly across engineering choices; it is not evidence that boosting is the right family here, since all four still sit inside the same tie band as ridge regression and support-vector regression.

concepts.term: Ridge regression and support-vector regression, as reference models
concepts.one_line: Two much simpler models kept in every comparison specifically so a fancier tree ensemble has to actually beat something, rather than merely being the only kind of thing tried.
concepts.explain:
A comparison of several sophisticated models against each other, with no simple baseline included, risks a subtle failure: none of them might be doing anything a much cheaper approach could not match just as well, and that would only become visible with a genuinely simple contender sitting in the same comparison. Ridge regression is that contender here. It fits the ordinary least-squares line but shrinks the size of its own coefficients, which keeps it stable when features are correlated or numerous relative to the number of rows, and it is cheap enough to tune with a full inner leave-one-subject-out search rather than the cheaper approximation the other seven families use.

Support-vector regression earns its place for a different reason. Given a radial-basis kernel, it is nonlinear, but it is not a tree, so its presence tests whether any apparent edge for the tree ensembles comes from being nonlinear at all, or specifically from being built out of trees.

Neither reference wins outright here, and neither loses badly either, which is itself informative: ridge's mean CCC sits mid-pack among all eight families and wins three of twenty cells outright, while SVR's mean is lower but it wins the most cells of any family, five of twenty, which shows how a family's average and its cell-win count can rank it in contradictory orders on the same cohort.
concepts.here: Ridge regression posts a mean CCC of $+0.0043$ (standard deviation $0.0303$) across Experiment 1's twenty cells and wins three of them; support-vector regression posts a lower mean of $+0.0007$ (standard deviation $0.0373$) but wins five, the most of any of the eight families. This is exactly the pattern the thesis's own text points to when it notes that the different summaries "rank them in orders that contradict one another."
concepts.example: If ridge regression is the best single choice for a visitor whose features happen to relate to their ratings in a fairly straight-line way, while support-vector regression better suits a visitor whose relationship bends, averaging across all twenty cells can leave ridge looking stronger overall even though SVR wins more individual cells, since the metric being averaged and the metric being counted answer different questions.
pitfalls: A reference model winning the most individual cells does not mean it has the best average performance across them; check which summary statistic, mean, median, or win count, a claim is actually resting on before trusting a ranking built from it.

Ridge and SVR are included specifically so the tree ensembles' selection is meaningful; dropping them from the comparison would remove the only check on whether the tree ensembles are earning their place over something considerably simpler.

concepts.term: CORAL: correlation alignment for domain adaptation
concepts.one_line: Reshaping every other visitor's training features, using nothing but simple statistics, so their spread and correlations match a new visitor's own, without needing a single label from that visitor or any retraining beyond the reshaping itself.
concepts.explain:
Physiological baselines differ between people for reasons that have nothing to do with affect, so a raw feature value is not directly comparable from one visitor to the next. A simple fix subtracts each person's own resting level, but that only ever recentres a feature; it does nothing about how much the feature varies, or how it relates to other features, both of which can also differ systematically from person to person.

CORAL generalises the same idea beyond a simple offset. It reshapes the entire training set's feature covariance, how much every feature varies and how every pair of features co-varies, to match the new visitor's own covariance, computed purely from that visitor's unlabelled features. It needs no retraining of the downstream model at all: it is a one-time, closed-form transformation applied to the training features before the standard model ever sees them, which is exactly what the original paper's own title, "return of frustratingly easy domain adaptation", is getting at: a direct computation rather than an iterative fitting procedure.

CORAL belongs to a family called domain adaptation, which explicitly uses the new person's own unlabelled data, in contrast with domain generalisation, which tries to learn features that hold across many people without ever seeing the new one at all.
concepts.here: "Every other visitor's training features are reshaped to match the held-out visitor's own covariance structure, using only that visitor's unlabelled data, by the closed-form CORAL method." It is the third of Experiment 5's four personalisation levers, and "a deep adversarial or contrastive alternative is not run at this cohort size", specifically because CORAL's closed-form nature needs no extra fitting step to apply.
concepts.example: If one visitor's tonic \ac{EDA} level and pupil diameter happen to be tightly correlated for reasons unrelated to affect, while the training cohort shows a weaker version of that same correlation, CORAL reshapes the training features so their EDA-pupil correlation matches that visitor's own, before the standard model, trained on the reshaped features, ever sees that visitor's actual rows.
pitfalls: CORAL only ever reshapes the feature distribution; it does nothing about the mapping from features to labels, so if that mapping itself differs between people, which this thesis's own variance decomposition suggests it does given how person-locked the ratings are, reshaping the features alone cannot fix the deeper problem.

Because it uses only unlabelled features from the new visitor, CORAL's effect cannot be checked against that visitor's own labels before it is applied; whether it helped or hurt is only visible after the fact, in the held-out score.

concepts.term: Ordinal targets and the discretisation of continuous affect
concepts.one_line: Turning a continuous 0-to-10 rating into a small number of ordered levels is not a technicality; it is a real modelling decision, because a person-relative scale may not mean the same thing from one visitor to the next, while the mere ordering, better or worse than a moment ago, plausibly does.
concepts.explain:
The obvious approach is to predict the rating directly, but one visitor's "6" for arousal need not mean what another's "6" means, since each visitor judges their own state against their own recent experience rather than a shared external yardstick. Predicting the raw number implicitly assumes a shared scale that may not exist. What every visitor's ratings do seem to share is order: agreeing that a given moment felt more aroused than the one before it, even if what "aroused" means as a raw number differs between them.

This motivates treating the target as ordinal, a small number of ordered levels, rather than either the raw continuous number or an unordered category. But discretising is not free. A reading that falls close to a level boundary is pushed wholly to one side of it, discarding the information that it was borderline; and equal-width levels assume every step feels equally large to the person rating, which need not hold on a subjective scale. How many levels to use is itself unsettled: findings disagree on whether reliability peaks at some middling count or keeps rising as the scale gets finer, and the finer the division, the fewer readings land in any one level.

Two genuinely different ways to arrive at levels are worth telling apart once continuous predictions already exist. A classifier can be trained directly against the binned target, so what is optimised matches what is later scored. Or a continuous regressor's existing predictions can be assigned to levels only after the fact, so nothing is refit, and the only thing that changes across a sweep of level counts is where the edges fall.
concepts.here: Experiments 1 and 2 in this thesis are regression problems, scored on the continuous rating; Experiments 3 through 5 are ordinal multiclass classification problems, swept over 3, 4, 5, 10, 12, 15, 18 and 20 levels. The discussion chapter reports that, expressed as a small number of ordered levels, the predictions show positive agreement on both valence slices and on neither arousal slice, and that fitting a classifier directly to the levels costs between $0.0587$ and $0.1046$ \ac{QWK} against reading the existing continuous predictions into levels after the fact. Twenty levels is scored and reported at every stage but never carried forward: each level would span half a scale point, finer than the annotation instrument resolves, and its $1/B$ chance floor for balanced accuracy sits an order of magnitude below every other candidate's.
concepts.example: A visitor whose raw arousal reading sits at $6.4$ on a ten-point scale, discretised into five equal-width levels of two points each, lands in the level covering $6$ to $8$. A nearly identical reading of $5.9$ lands in the level covering $4$ to $6$ instead, even though the two raw readings are barely different, purely because $6.0$ happens to be the boundary between the two levels.
pitfalls: Discretising the target changes what can be scored, through chance-corrected agreement statistics built for ordered levels, without necessarily enlarging the real signal underneath it; an ordinal score moving is not, on its own, evidence that more affect was recovered, since the level marginals can shift for reasons unrelated to prediction quality.

A finer level count is not automatically more informative: at 20 levels, each level spans half a scale point, finer than the annotation instrument itself resolves, and its very low chance floor ($1/20$) makes any positive-looking balanced accuracy there easy to over-read.

concepts.one_line: The way the variance components in a mixed model are estimated here, chosen because plain maximum likelihood estimates them too small.
concepts.explain:
A mixed model has to estimate two different kinds of quantity at once: the fixed part, here just an overall average rating, and the variances of the random parts. Plain maximum likelihood estimates the variances as though the fixed part had been known in advance, when in fact it was estimated from the same data. Degrees of freedom get spent twice, and the variance estimates come out biased low.

Restricted maximum likelihood fixes that. Instead of maximising the likelihood of the data, it maximises the likelihood of a set of residual contrasts constructed to be orthogonal to the fixed part, so the degrees of freedom spent estimating it are paid back. The result is variance components that are approximately unbiased.

The everyday analogue is dividing by $n-1$ rather than $n$ when computing a sample variance. That correction exists for exactly the same reason: the mean was estimated from the data, so one degree of freedom is already gone. REML is the mixed-model generalisation of it.
concepts.here: Experiment 4 fits a crossed mixed model to the attended rows and reports its variance components as the headline result, so the estimator's bias is not a nuisance but a direct threat to the finding. REML is used for every fit, including the per-feature ones. Because the model is intercept-only and runs on thousands of rows, plain maximum likelihood would land in nearly the same place, so the choice is not carrying the result; it is simply the unbiased estimator for the thing being reported. The thesis does not rely on it alone: a one-way eta-squared ratio, a method-of-moments estimate of the same quantity, is computed on identical rows and reported beside it.
concepts.example: On rcea valence the crossed model returns a person share of $36.4\%$, a painting share of $1.5\%$ and a residual of $62.1\%$. The one-way eta-squared on the same rows puts the painting share at $0.80\%$, the same order by a different route.
pitfalls: REML likelihoods cannot be compared across models with different fixed effects; only one fixed structure is fitted here, so the restriction costs nothing.
With only five paintings the painting component is poorly determined however it is estimated, which the bootstrap interval and the leave-one-painting-out refit are there to show.
Classical ANOVA variance-component formulas assume balance and can return negative estimates on unbalanced data; this design is unbalanced and crossed, which is a second reason not to use them.

concepts.one_line: Two grouping factors are crossed when any level of one can appear with any level of the other, which is the case for visitors and paintings here.
concepts.explain:
A nested factor belongs to exactly one level of the factor above it. Pupils are nested in classes: a given pupil is in one class and no other, so the class effect and the pupil effect sit in a hierarchy.

Crossed factors do not nest. In this exhibition every visitor could view every painting, so a painting is not the property of one visitor and a visitor is not the property of one painting. Both effects apply to the same observation from different directions, and the model lets each vary independently rather than placing one inside the other.

Crossing does not require that every combination actually occurred. The model is fitted on whatever pairs are present, and the observed coverage is reported separately so a reader can see how complete the grid is.
concepts.here: Experiment 4 fits $y = \mu + u_{\text{person}} + u_{\text{painting}} + \varepsilon$ on the attended rows, with the visitor and the painting as two independent random intercepts. Three visitors contributed no attended second at all, so the grid is incomplete, and the fit uses the pairs that exist. With paintings as targets and visitors as raters, the painting share of this model is exactly the intraclass correlation reported alongside it.
concepts.example: Twenty rcea visitors and five paintings give at most 100 visitor-painting cells. Averaged to one rating per cell, the painting share falls to $0.0\%$ and the person share rises to $65.7\%$.
pitfalls: Fitting a crossed design as if it were nested attributes the second factor's variance to the first and inflates it.
In statsmodels a crossed model is expressed as one dummy group with two variance components, not as two grouping factors.
The returned components are in response-variance units already and are ordered alphabetically, not in the order they were declared.

concepts.one_line: Deciding which painting a visitor was attending at each second, from the engine's gaze ray, a proximity bound and a dwell rule.
concepts.explain:
The virtual-reality engine casts a ray along the visitor's line of sight and records whichever object it strikes, with the time the look began, how long it lasted, and how far the visitor stood from the object. That alone is not attendance: the ray registers a painting glimpsed from across the room exactly as it registers one the visitor walked up to.

Two conditions are therefore placed on a record. Proximity keeps only records made within a bound read off the distribution of recorded viewing distances rather than chosen in advance. Dwell applies to viewing episodes rather than to single records, since one record is far shorter than a second: consecutive records naming the same painting are merged and an episode shorter than a second is discarded.

A record failing either condition contributes no label at all rather than a weaker one, and a second inside no surviving episode is excluded from the localised evaluation.
concepts.here: The bound is the ninety-fifth percentile of all recorded viewing distances, $2.81$\,m on this cohort, which keeps $95{,}990$ of $101{,}043$ records. Dwell removes far more: merging gives 1,862 episodes of which 1,177 survive the one-second rule, so $36.8\%$ are discarded as glances. What remains is $7{,}986$ attended seconds on rcea, $63.1\%$ of that stream, and $4{,}134$ on retro, $58.9\%$. Three visitors contributed no attended second at all.
pitfalls: In the source export the column named distance holds a room coordinate and the column named gaze holds the viewing distance in metres; reading the wrong one silently destroys the proximity rule.
A fixed metre threshold is a free parameter; taking it from a percentile of the observed distances removes the choice but ties the bound to this cohort.
The same records resolve sub-painting regions, which this thesis does not use; mixing the two scopes would double-count seconds.

concepts.one_line: Three ways of adapting a visitor-general model to one visitor, differing in what they adapt and in how much of that visitor's own annotation they consume.
concepts.explain:
A model trained across people carries only what those people share. Where the response is largely individual, adapting the model to the person in front of it is the obvious remedy, and the adaptations differ in what they touch.

Adapting the features means removing each visitor's own resting level, estimated from their unlabelled signal before the visit properly begins, so that two visitors' features become comparable. It asks nothing of the visitor beyond their signals.

Adapting the training data means folding a short labelled slice of the held-out visitor's own visit into the population model's training and refitting. It bounds what personalisation could achieve if annotation were free, and it is the only lever that requires the visitor to annotate.

Adapting the target means recomputing the level boundaries from a visitor's own ratings rather than fixing them at the same absolute position for everyone. It leaves the regressor untouched, so any movement it produces is in what the levels mean and not in the prediction.
concepts.here: Experiment 5 runs all three against a same-run reference on one common set of rows. Pooled agreement rises in 21 of the 24 lever-by-slice cells and balanced accuracy in 20, yet none of the 48 paired tests survives correction and the smallest adjusted value is $q=0.138$. The warm-up is the only lever with an ordered response in the amount of annotation it is given, monotone on three of the four slices and reaching $+0.3019$ at 180 seconds.
pitfalls: A lever that moves an ordinal score while leaving the continuous score untouched is shifting the level marginals, not predicting any second better.
The person-relative target is not label-free: the held-out visitor's boundaries come from an early slice of their own ratings.
Comparing levers against each other requires them to be scored on the same rows, since each consumes a different part of the session.

sources.title: Sun and Saenko (2016), Return of frustratingly easy domain adaptation

concepts.one_line: A mixed model whose random component is estimated at zero has not divided the variance at all, and its shares describe that collapse rather than the data.
concepts.explain:
A variance cannot be negative, so the estimate is constrained at zero from below. When the data carry little evidence for a grouping factor, the fit can drive that factor's variance onto the boundary. The remaining components then absorb everything the collapsed one should have held.

The resulting shares still sum to one hundred per cent and still look like a decomposition, which is what makes the failure easy to miss. A category mean computed over such fits reports how often the model collapsed, not how the variance divides.

The defence is to detect the collapse and exclude it, and to report how many fits were excluded so a reader can judge how much of the category the remaining fits represent.
concepts.here: Experiment 4 runs the crossed split on each of the 122 carried features per stream. A fit placing either random component below $0.05\%$ is recorded as degenerate and left out of its category's mean. Thirty-five of the 244 per-feature fits collapsed this way, unevenly across categories: the cross-sensor block lost five of eight on retro, the electrodermal features six of ten.
pitfalls: Shares summing to one hundred per cent is not evidence that the fit succeeded.
Category means over very different numbers of features are not equally precise: eighty-eight acoustic features against one content feature.
A convergence warning and a boundary estimate are different failures, and a fit can reach the boundary while converging cleanly.
